title: The Pedagogue: Prelude and Fugue No.1, Book I
content_blocks: This piece was the first of all of the preludes and fugues that I wrote—the one that started it all off (see My Two Books of Preludes and Fugues Have Been Released!, June 20, 2025). At the time I felt this obligation to prove myself—fugue writing has been an essential part of music education for centuries—and one of the ways that I tried to achieve that was by packing in as much as I could into this one fugue. It has stretti (the narrowing or “hurrying up” of the timing of the entrance of the answer relative to the subject), various compressions and decompressions of the pace of the subject entries, as well as inversions of the subject. I felt like I was teaching the world what I could do, so when I gave monikers to the first group of ten preludes and fugues more than a year later, I called this pair “The Pedagogue.”

Yet, at the same time there is so much that is beautiful, dreamy, and even jazzy in this pair. It uses the same arithmetic, expanding-and-contracting scale that No.8 uses (see The Majestic One?, August 19, 2025), and has some of the same built-in harmonic beauty—beautiful triads and seventh chords juxtaposed in unusual ways—as No.8. Throughout, the idea of expanding and contracting can be heard in multiple ways: not only built-in to the scale used, but in terms of the size of the gestures, and in the accelerating and decelerating rhythms, which contribute to the jazzy feel in the Prelude. The Fugue is more serious, but its callbacks to the Prelude soften its seriousness.

Michael Mizrahi might be the perfect person to interpret these pieces. His discography includes a wide range of pieces, from intricate to simple, contemporary modern to jazz-inflected. He does not disappoint, here: I love his performances of both the Prelude and the Fugue, as you can see in this combined video—they are a perfect way to start off this collection.
